I am 73 years old and I farm alone, so every decision I make this year must spare my back and my breath. My 3 mu of land in Quzhou County is small but familiar—after 50 years I know every lump of soil. I will plant 2 mu with winter wheat, follow it immediately with summer maize on the same 2 mu, and keep 1 mu for cotton because cotton cash pays for my fertilizer and medicine. I use an improved wheat seed and rotary tillage before sowing; wheat must have three irrigations from my well—before winter dormancy, at green-up, and at heading—plus about 16 kg nitrogen, 8 kg phosphorus, and 5 kg potassium per mu, which has been enough for this plot for decades. I will spray wheat twice for weeds and insects because I cannot carry heavy tanks more than that. For summer maize I buy hybrid seed and plant it no-till the same day the wheat comes off; there is no time to plough before frost threatens, and at my age less digging is better. Maize gets roughly 12 kg nitrogen, 3 kg phosphorus, and 3 kg potassium per mu, with two irrigations when the summer rains fail at tasseling and grain filling, and two pesticide sprays. For cotton I also use hybrid seed, rotary till in early spring, and apply about 10 kg nitrogen, 5 kg phosphorus, and 5 kg potassium per mu. Cotton needs water at flowering and boll-setting, so I irrigate three times, and I will spray pesticides six times because the bollworm is relentless—six times is all my legs can manage, but I know the crop will fail if I do less. I expect 450 kg of wheat grain, 500 kg of maize grain, and 300 kg of seed cotton per mu. These are modest numbers, but after half a century I know exactly what this land and this old body can deliver.

I keep 2 mu in the reliable wheat-maize rotation and 1 mu in cotton for cash income. I use moderate fertilizer rates based on 50 years of observing this soil, limit irrigation to essential timings to save well-pumping labor and cost, and apply pesticides only as often as I can physically carry the sprayer—fewer on grain crops, more on cotton because bollworm pressure is unavoidable. I choose rotary tillage for wheat and cotton to save energy, and no-tillage for maize to save critical time between wheat harvest and frost.
